classification.difficultyReason: Guided theorem proof explicitly supplies both angle expressions and asks to equate them, then transfer the rectangle result to a rhombus. Requires connecting familiar properties, not finding a new construction.

content.prompt: Prove that: A cyclic parallelogram is a rectangle. In the cyclic parallelogram ABCD, let $\angle A=\theta$.

spec.description: All four vertices concyclic. Opposite sides marked parallel using distinct single/double arrows, theta at A. No new right-angle mark or numerical restriction supplied.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Give reasons why $\angle C=180^\circ-\theta$ and why $\angle C=\theta$.

answer.short: Cyclic opposite angles are supplementary; parallelogram opposite angles are equal.
answer.worked: Since ABCD is cyclic, $\angle A+\angle C=180^\circ$, so $\angle C=180^\circ-\theta$. Since ABCD is a parallelogram, its opposite angles are equal, so $\angle C=\angle A=\theta$.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Hence, prove that ABCD is a rectangle.

answer.short: All four angles are right angles, so ABCD is a rectangle.
answer.worked: Equating the two expressions for angle C gives $180^\circ-\theta=\theta$, so $\theta=90^\circ$. Thus $\angle A=\angle C=90^\circ$. Adjacent angles of a parallelogram are supplementary, so B and D are right angles too. Therefore ABCD is a rectangle.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Use part a to prove that: A cyclic rhombus is a square.

answer.short: It is both a rectangle and a rhombus, hence a square.
answer.worked: A rhombus is a parallelogram with four equal sides. If it is cyclic, part a makes it a rectangle. It therefore has four right angles and four equal sides, so it is a square.
